# Impact of the COVID-19 Pandemic on Childhood Lead Testing and Blood Lead Levels

**Authors:** Ryan C.L. Brewster; Amee D. Azad; Keith Acosta; Amy Starmer; Eli Sprecher; Corinna Rea; Kathryn P. Gray; Shannon Regan; Joseph Wilson; Frehiwot Bayuh; Noah Buncher; Marissa Hauptman

**Affiliations:** Department of Pediatrics (RCL Brewster, K Acosta, A Starmer, E Sprecher, C Rea, KP Gray, S Reagan, F Bayuh, and M Hauptman), Boston Children’s Hospital, Boston, Mass; Department of Pediatrics (RCL Brewster and N Buncher), Boston Medical Center, Boston, Mass; Department of Ophthalmology (AD Azad), Massachusetts Eye and Ear, Boston, Mass; Department of Pediatrics (RCL Brewster, K Acosta, A Starmer, E Sprecher, C Rea, and M Hauptman), Harvard Medical School, Boston, Mass; Institutional Centers of Clinical and Translational Research (KP Gray), Boston Children’s Hospital, Boston, Mass; Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (J Wilson), Boston, Mass; Region 1 New England Pediatric Environmental Health Specialty Unit (PEHSU) (N Buncher and M Hauptman), Boston, Mass

## Abstract

To evaluate the effect of the COVID-19 pandemic on childhood lead testing and blood lead levels.

A retrospective analysis of lead tests and results was performed across 3 urban medical centers during the pre-COVID-19 (March 10, 2019–March 9, 2020) and COVID-19 (March 10, 2020–March 10, 2022) periods. Interrupted time series analysis with quasi-Poisson regression was used to evaluate changes in lead testing between study periods. The relationship between sociodemographic features with detectable (≧2 μg/dL) and elevated (≧3.5 μg/dL) blood lead levels (BLLs) was assessed with multivariable logistic regression.

Among a total of 16,364 lead tests across 10,362 patients, weekly testing rates significantly decreased during COVID-19 (relative risk (RR) 0.64, 95% (confidence interval) CI 0.53–0.78). Census tracts with the greatest proportion of pre-1950s housing had a stronger association with detectable BLLs during the COVID-19 period (pre-COVID-19 adjusted odds ratio (aOR) 1.73, 95% CI 1.35–2.20; aOR 2.58, 95% CI 2.13–3.12; interaction P value .014). When limited to 1 year following COVID-19 (March 10, 2020–March 10, 2021), the association between both elevated BLLs (pre-COVID-19: aOR 1.49, 95% CI 0.87–2.53; COVID-19: aOR 3.51, 95% CI 1.98–6.25; interaction P value .032) and detectable BLLs with pre-1950s housing were greater during the COVID-19 period (pre-COVID-19: aOR 1.73, 95% CI 1.35–2.20; COVID-19: aOR 2.56, 95% CI 1.95–3.34; interaction P value .034).

The COVID-19 pandemic led to a significant reduction in lead surveillance and magnified the effect of known risk factors for lead exposure. Concerted clinical, public health, and community advocacy are needed to address care gaps and excess cases of lead poisoning.

No safe level of lead in the body has been identified. Adverse neurodevelopmental and intellectual outcomes have been observed with blood lead levels (BLLs) as low as 1 μg/dL.1,2 Environmental regulations have dramatically reduced environmental, commercial, and residential sources of lead over the past 50 years; however, recent evidence suggests that more than half of children in the United States have detectable BLLs.3 The burden of lead poisoning is not uniform; families residing in older housing are disproportionately affected, particularly low-income, racially-minoritized, and immigrant populations due to the disinvestment in communities subjected to historical housing discrimination.4–6

The early phases of the COVID-19 pandemic caused significant disruptions to pediatric primary care.7 Regular assessment of BLLs in children is critical to mobilize public health resources for families at risk for lead poisoning; however, the extent to which the pandemic impacted BLL testing has not been well-characterized. In addition to changes in clinical practice, COVID-19 introduced sweeping measures to mitigate the community spread of disease.8 Social distancing and shelter-in-place orders resulted in increased time spent at home, potentially magnifying residential lead exposures for already vulnerable children.

Toward this end, we conducted a study of BLL testing and results in 3 urban medical center sites in Boston, Massachusetts, during the COVID-19 pandemic. We hypothesized that rates of lead testing would precipitously decline at the onset of the public health emergency, with a gradual recovery to prepandemic levels, and that the community burden of detectable and elevated BLLs would increase in populations with known risk factors.

## Methods

This was a retrospective analysis of 2 urban academic medical center sites (including 1 freestanding children’s hospital) and 1 hospital-supported community health center in Boston, Massachusetts. We abstracted lead test and sociodemographic data from the electronic medical record. Census tract-level poverty and pre-1950s housing characteristics were derived from the 2020 U.S. Census American Community Survey and linked to patient residential addresses.9 Poverty levels and the proportion of pre-1950s housing were divided into quartiles (quartile 1: lowest, quartile 4: highest). Estimates of pre-1950s housing were chosen to align with the early legislative provisions to mitigate lead-based paint in homes leading up to the national ban in 1978.10 Eligibility criteria were all children < 18 years old who underwent lead testing at study sites between March 10, 2019, to March 10, 2022. March 10, 2020, corresponding to the state of emergency declaration in Massachusetts, was designated as the index date separating the pre-COVID-19 (March 10, 2019–March 9, 2020) and COVID-19 (March 10, 2020–March 10, 2022) periods.

Interrupted time series analysis with a quasi-Poisson regression model was performed to evaluate differences in BLL testing between the pre-COVID-19 and COVID-19 study periods overall and stratified by sociodemographic characteristics. The regression model used the weekly number of BLL tests as the dependent variable and weekly time trend and study period as independent variables to determine the differences in decline in lead testing in the COVID-19 period. A wash in period was not included given the abrupt nature of the public health emergency.

Multivariable logistic regression models were employed to assess the relationship between detectable (≧2 μg/dL) and elevated BLLs (≧3.5 μg/dL), in accordance with the current Centers for Disease Control and Prevention blood lead reference value, and sociodemographic features, including age, race and ethnicity, housing quartile, and poverty quartile.11 Whether the relationship between model covariates and the likelihood of detectable or elevated BLLs differed during the COVID-19 pandemic was assessed with an interaction term between the COVID-19 study period and each sociodemographic characteristic. Given the potential for repeated lead testing over time, only the highest BLL from each study period for each patient was used to define the outcome measure of detectable and elevated BLL status. A subgroup analysis limiting the COVID-19 period to March 10, 2020–March 10, 2021, was also performed to capture the more acute effects of the pandemic on community BLL burden.

All analyses were performed in R, version 4.1.3 and statistical significance was considered as P < .05. The study was exempted from Boston Children’s Hospital institutional review board approval.

## Results

Between March 10, 2019, and March 10, 2022, a total of 16,364 serum lead tests among 10,362 patients were performed at the study locations, 5726 (34.9%) and 10,638 (65%) of which occurred during the pre- and COVID-19 periods, respectively (Table 1). Lead tests were most frequently obtained among children who were 1 to 2.9 years (44.9%), male (51.7%), and Black, non-Latine (41.8%).

The mean number of weekly lead tests significantly decreased from 110 ((standard deviation) SD 20.7) to 101.3 (SD 39.2) (relative risk (RR) 0.64, 95% (confidence interval) CI 0.53–0.78) during the COVID-19 period (eFigure 1, Table 2). There was a statistically significant reduction in mean weekly tests across all housing quartiles, poverty quartiles, and race and ethnicity groups with the exception of White, non-Latine children (RR 1.40, 95% CI 0.98–1.99).

Relative to the lowest quartile of pre-1950s housing, detectable BLLs were significantly associated with increasing pre-1950s housing quartile (Q2: adjusted odds ratio (aOR) 1.40, 95% CI 1.09–1.81; Q3: aOR 1.64, 95% CI 1.27–2.11; Q4: aOR 1.73, 95% CI 1.35–2.20) (Table 3). A similar pattern was observed for elevated BLLs ≧ 3.5 μg/dL (Q2: aOR 1.04, 95% CI 0.58–1.86; Q3: aOR 1.73, 95% CI 1.02–2.94; Q4: aOR 1.49, 95% CI 0.87–2.53).

There was a significant interaction between the highest quartile of pre-1950s housing and the COVID-19 period for detectable BLLs (pre-COVID-19: aOR 1.73, 95% CI 1.35–2.20; COVID-19: aOR 2.58, 95% CI 2.13–3.12; interaction P value .014), but not for elevated BLLs ≧ 3.5 μg/dL (pre-COVID-19: aOR 1.49, 95% CI 0.87–2.53; COVID-19: aOR 2.57, 95% CI 1.69–3.9; interaction P value .112). When limited to 1 year following COVID-19 (March 10, 2020–March 10, 2021), the highest pre-1950s housing quartile was more strongly associated with both detectable BLLs (pre-COVID-19: aOR 1.73, 95% CI 1.35–2.20; COVID-19: aOR 2.56, 95% CI 1.95–3.34; interaction P value .034) and elevated BLLs (pre-COVID-19: aOR 1.49, 95% CI 0.87–2.53; COVID-19: aOR 3.51, 95% CI 1.98–6.25; interaction P value .032) during the COVID-19 study period (Table 3).

## Discussion

In this retrospective analysis of 3 urban medical center sites, the COVID-19 pandemic impacted both surveillance of and risk of lead exposure. We found a significant reduction in the number of weekly lead tests during the pandemic. Furthermore, the association between detectable and elevated BLL with older housing became even more pronounced.

Our results extend prior work showing that COVID-19 disrupted many dimensions of pediatric primary care.7,12,13 Decreased health care utilization caused gaps in essential health promotion and disease prevention activities, with widening disparities by race and socioeconomic status. Concerns have been raised, for example, about the resurgence in vaccine-preventable illnesses resulting from delays in or forgone childhood immunizations.14 Similarly, it is plausible that missed blood lead testing accelerated the progression of both new and known cases of lead poisoning.

BLL testing declined precipitously at the onset of the pandemic, consistent with trends observed in a national Centers for Disease Control and Prevention report.15 While there remained a deficit at the end of the study period, weekly rates of BLL testing had returned to pre-COVID-19 levels. Trends in vaccine administration and preventive visits have followed analogous recoveries.7 These rebounds may highlight the resilience of core primary care functions in the face of acute and dynamic public health threats. That said, concerted efforts are needed to address lost care from the pandemic. Several multilevel strategies have been proposed, primarily in the context of catch-up immunizations. These include outreach and reminders, incorporating health maintenance into sick visits, and collaborations with schools, childcare centers, and other community organizations.14

The observed effect modification of the pandemic on established risk factors for lead exposure is alarming. In Massachusetts, multiple shelter-in-place advisories were implemented through 2020 in response to waves of COVID-19 variants. In parallel were frequent school closures, travel restrictions, and adherence to social distancing practices. As intended, families were largely confined to their homes. Our findings suggest an unanticipated consequence, heightened exposure to residential lead sources. A substantial portion of the housing stock in older metropolitan areas, such as Boston, was constructed prior to the commercial bans on lead-containing paints. Poor housing conditions disproportionately fall on low socioeconomic status and racially minoritized communities due to historical redlining and de facto segregation.16 In this setting, community mitigation measures may have amplified environmental vulnerabilities among families living in older buildings, allowing greater cumulative contact with contaminated dust and soil. They may have also led to delays in environmental investigations and remediation along with decreased access to essential services, such as Early Intervention. It is altogether unsurprising that we observed the strongest impact of housing on detectable and elevated BLLs within the first year of the pandemic with a diminishing “dose effect” over time as restrictions were lifted. Still, these hazards remain unaddressed for many families. Worsening inequities in lead exposure reiterate the need for targeted clinical and public health outreach based on known environmental vulnerabilities. Efforts should be made to enact state-level policies to strengthen secondary prevention strategies and support funding mechanisms for homeowners and landlords to mitigate lead and other habitability concerns.17 Additionally, future shelter-in-place directives must also carefully weigh the risk of indirect harms and put into place abatement measures to protect at-risk households.

Our study has limitations. The analysis was restricted to a single metropolitan area and results may therefore not be generalizable to other settings. For example, the lack of differences in lead testing rates across sociodemographic features likely reflects the limited catchment area and relatively uniform access to care. These areas warrant further exploration with more longitudinal, national-level studies.

Altogether, the COVID-19 pandemic may have exacerbated inequities in childhood lead exposure and prevention, potentially compromising years of hard-fought progress. Pediatric clinics must collaborate with policymakers, families, and community advocates to redress care gaps and the excess burden of lead poisoning while proactively strengthening primary care services in anticipation of the next public health crisis.
